name: F-MO H 196
summary: F-MO H 196; c. 1280 and later. late 13th-early 14th century; A note at the bottom of f. 1 shows that the MS belonged to President Bouhier in 1721, and had the signature F. 61 in his library. He is the first known owner and was of Dijon origin. In 1781 the codex went to Clairvaux Abbey, then to Bar-sur-Aube, and then to Saint-Loup de Troyes on the sale of Bouhier's library. In 1804 Prunelle and Chardon-la-Rochette, two officials looking for important provincial manuscripts suitable for the Bibliothèque Nationale in Paris, saw Mo, but Prunelle, a teacher at the Ecole de Médecine in Montpellier, was able to turn over 300 fine MSS to the school there.

name: F-Pnm Français 146 (Roman de Fauvel)
summary: F-Pnm Français 146 (Roman de Fauvel); Early 14th century, c.1316.; The only manuscript containing the Roman de Fauvel to include the very extensive musical as well as textual interpolations inserted by Raoul Chaillou de Pesstain. Original 'Roman' written by Gervais du Bus;  the interpolations were completed in 1316 or soon after.
archive: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Département des Manuscrits

name: F-Pnm NAF 23190 (Trémoille)
summary: F-Pnm NAF 23190 (Trémoille); 1376; Fragment consisting of only one bifolio of a once much larger collection. Contains an index (f.1r) and four motets (two incomplete), originally forming the outer bifolio of first quaternion of a manuscript of 48 folios (presumably six quaternions). Present note of ownership reads 'Iste liber motetorum pertinet capelle illustrissimi principis Philippi ducis Burgondie et comitis Flandrie'; last six words are in a later hand over erasure. Erased text partly legible under ultraviolet light: '… quem scripsit Michael \[new line\] de …ia, ejusdem principis capellanus, millesimo trecentesimo sexto'. Name replaced by 'Philippi' is illegible. Listed as no. 64 in the 1420 Dijon chapel inventory of John the Fearless, Duke of Burgundy, as 'Item ung grant livre plat, noté, de plusieurs motez, virelaiz et balades qui commence: Colla jugo fidere \[sic\], et se fenit Bis dicitur'; possibly larger of two motet books listed in 1404 chapel inventory of Philip the Bold. Bifolio used for account book cover in 1512 by George de la Trémoïlle, who would have received MS as part of the property of Charles the Bold that Louis XI gave him in 1477. Bifolio remained property of Trémoïlle family until acquired by Bibliothèque Nationale de France c.1970.
archive: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Département des Manuscrits

name: I-IV MS CXV (115) (Ivrea Codex)
summary: I-IV MS CXV (115) (Ivrea Codex); 14th century; Consists mainly of motets (37) and mass pieces (25) with some secular songs (11 Rondeaux and Virelais and 4 chaces); there are also 2 two-part discants with different texts in each voice, 2 textless pieces and a motet-like quodlibet. Besseler discerns two mains hands: the first for the main pieces on folios 1v-35v and 36v-37, the second for those on folios 37v-51, while other hands seem to have added pieces not belonging to the corpus. The manuscript seems to have been written for practical use, since there is no useless ornament; it is also well worn. Single motet parts are usually written across whole pages, the Tr on the verso and the Mot on the recto, though mass movements and old motets may be written with the pages divided into two by a line down the middle. Short secular songs and other shorter works are usually written in the space left at the bottom of pages occupied by larger works. Discovered by Borghezio in 1921; appears to have been in Ivrea since the 14th century. Its liturgical connections and central French repertoire, together with direct references to Pope Clement VI, suggest an origin in Avignon shortly after 1360. It might have been brought to Ivrea by one of the three French priests mentioned in the records there between 1361 and 1384.

name: CH-Fcu LE 15/3
summary: CH-Fcu LE 15/3; 14th century; An incunabulum (Hain *9002) containing sermons by Hugo de Prato. A music-bearing folio has been cut across the middle into two pieces and was stuck inside the binding and over the flyleaves to strengthen the binding. Now the two pieces have been removed and rejoined: they reveal a motet MS similar to I-IV. The rubricator has added the name 'Guillermus de Mascandio' in red letters, following the very fine guide-script in the right-hand margin. The arrangement is in two columns for Tr and Mot and two continuous lines below for the end of the Tr and the complete T. The two bottom lines on the page are the conclusion of a Mot from the preceding (lost) verso. The rubricator proceeds in exactly the same manner on the verso with the name 'Philippus de Vitriaco' as he did with Machaut on the recto. In this work the Tr runs over into the continuous lines reserved for T and ContraT, while the T uses up the last two Mot columns.

name: B-Br MS 19606
summary: B-Br MS 19606; early 14th century, certainly after 1314.; The manuscript is mostly written in two columns, but one voice may well cover the whole width of the page if the Tr is longer than the Mot, etc. Most of the music appears to be the work of a single scribe, but the two isolated, undesignated voices of no. 10 are a later addition.

name: GB-DRc MS C.I.20
summary: GB-DRc MS C.I.20; mid-14th century; The main contents are Huguitio's Summa super derivationibus and Isidore's Etymologies written in 2 cols. 4 flyleaves at the beginning and 4 at the end (like Ob 7) contain three- and four-part, apparently English motets. Concordances prove that the last 4 folios contain predominantly French works, including some in the French language and others by Philippe de Vitry. The 2 pieces in three-part score on f. 4v appear to be a slightly later addition to the repertory of Petronian motets, for they use Ars Nova notation.
source_type: Codex fragment (polyphony), still with host manuscript

name: F-CA MS B 1328
summary:
F-CA MS B 1328; 13th and 14th centuries; A collection of pages from a number of different manuscripts, many removed from books and manuscripts where they were re-used as guard pages. The fragments were assembled into a portfolio prior to 1891; in 1967 the pages were cleaned and restored, and re-assembled. The most significant fragments are those which were part of a manuscript of motets and mass movements (described by Lerch) and others which were part of what "appears to be the earliest 14th century manuscript containing chansons" (Hasselman, p.25).

The RISM description has now been superseded in several respects: Fallows discovered several more related folios still bound into other volumes in the library;  FallowsCA  suggests that the volumes were bound at the end of the 15th century, probably for the new library of St Sepulchre erected by Guillaume Courtois, abbot 1482-1503). Additionally Fallows and Lerch were able to show that the fragments forming Lerch's 'series I' (which she labelled F-CA(n) - neu/new - collected [here][1]) were originally bifolios from a manuscript that was disassembled to re-use as guard pages, so that a partial reconstruction of the manuscript was possible (see Lerch). Further, locating the volumes from which the earlier fragments had been removed, Fallows found that 'mirror-image' offsets of the glued-down side of the fragments remained on the inside of the covers from which the fragments had been detached, often in a more legible state than the fragments themselves. 

Related fragments used as binding materials, or their remaining 'mirror-image' offsets, are catalogued in the following incunabula: [B56][2], [B135][3], [B144][4], [B145][5], [B165][6], [B166][7], [C52][8]; and in the following manuscripts: [B220][9], [B322][10], [B447][11], [C647][12]. 

Hasselman, FallowsCA, and Lerch have all proposed different groupings and ordering of the folios. (See also 'foliation' below.) Hasselman identified 4 main groups of 14th century fragments,  plus the fragments of Adam de la Halle and Gregorian chant. Lerch largely accepts her groupings, though re-assesses the first based on Fallows' discoveries. She groups the fragments into 7 series:  
 - I: "[manuscript F-CA(n)][13]", an expanded and re-ordered version of Hasselman's CaB1, containing motets and mass movements, and comprising 7 pages from this collection and 9 which remain in other books; a virtaul representation of this 'original' manuscript can be found at [F-CA(n)][1]. 
 - II: a group of polyphonic chansons, Hasselman's CaB2 & CaB3 totalling 9 pages from this collection together with 2 newly-discovered pages from Inc C 52, probably from 2 (or more) different manuscripts;
 - III: a small group of polyphonic songs which remain in Ms B322;
 - IV: an Agnus and some chansons on 2 pages of this collection, Hasselman's CaC;
 - V: 4 pieces by Adam de la Halle on one page in this collection;
 - VI: 2 pages of Gregorian chant in this collection, Hasselman's CaA;
 - VII: 2 pages of monophonic Trouvere songs located by Fallows in Inc B135

The DIAMM inventory of this collection therefore includes much of Lerch's series I and II, and all of series IV, V and VI; with the remainder being catalogued in the other books where the pages remain.

name: GB-Cu Add. 2764(1)
summary: GB-Cu Add. 2764(1); 1420s-30s; Cambridge, University Library, MS Add. 2764 (1). A single parchment leaf, first mentioned by Manfred F. Bukofzer in Renaissance News 2 (1949), p.65, and more recently in EEC, pp.294–5. Contrary to all received statements, this (a) contains bits of two carols, not one, and (b) is not part of a carol roll, because there is absolutely no trace of sewing-holes, because the writing on the verso has a margin that proves that there is nothing lost at the bottom of the page, and because text is actually underlaid to the contratenor at the bottom of the page, even though the music needs a tenor below it. The music, in full-black notation and in perfect time, looks as though from the 1420s or 30s.
